name: Holi (Festival of Colours)
description: Holi celebrates the love between Krishna and Radha, central to Mathura and Braj region culture. The festival lasts a week, with Lathmar Holi at Barsana and Nandgaon featuring women playfully hitting men with sticks (symbolising Krishna's village pranks). Mathura's celebrations include colour throwing, bonfires (Holika Dahan), Dahi Handi (breaking pots of curd/butter), and Ras Leela dances depicting Krishna and Radha's love story.
significance: Mathura is Krishna's birthplace, making Holi a deeply spiritual festival tied to his divine leela (divine play). The Braj region is the iconic heart of Holi celebrations in India, drawing hundreds of thousands of pilgrims annually.

name: Krishna Janmashtami (Birth of Krishna)
description: Janmashtami celebrates Lord Krishna's birth in Mathura at midnight. Over 800,000 devotees gather annually for prayers, fasting, and Dahi Handi competitions where youth form human pyramids to break pots of curd and butter. Ras Leela performances, temple decorations, midnight aarti (worship ceremonies), and distribution of sweets mark the festival. Vrindavan celebrations extend for 16 days.
significance: Mathura is Krishna's birthplace (Krishna Janma Bhoomi temple), making this the most sacred site for Janmashtami celebrations in India. The festival is central to Hindu devotional practice and Braj culture.

name: Durga Puja
approximate_date: September-October (lunar calendar; 2026: late September / early October)
description: UNESCO-inscribed Intangible Cultural Heritage festival celebrating the victory of Goddess Durga over evil. Kolkata hosts thousands of elaborate pandals (temporary structures), cultural performances, Dhunuchi Naach (incense stick dances), food stalls, and processions. The festival lasts 10 days, with the final five (Shashti to Vijaya Dashami) being most prominent. In 2022, the collective economy was ₹50,000 crores, employing three lakh people.
significance: Durga Puja is the largest, most iconic festival in Kolkata, deeply embedded in Bengali identity and spiritual practice. Recognised by UNESCO (December 2021) for its cultural significance.

name: Kali Puja
approximate_date: November (new moon day of Kartika month; 2026: November 8)
description: Festival dedicated to the fierce goddess Kali, celebrated especially in Kolkata's cremation grounds where she is believed to dwell. The Kalighat Temple and Dakshineswar Kali Temple (associated with Sri Ramakrishna) are major centres of worship. Rituals at midnight, hymn singing, and offerings mark the celebration. Kali Puja coincides with Diwali night in Hindu tradition.
significance: Kali Puja is deeply significant in Bengali Hindu tradition, particularly in Kolkata and surrounding areas (Barasat, Basirhat, Tamluk). The goddess represents divine power, protection, and fierce compassion.

name: Poila Boishakh (Bengali New Year)
description: Bengali New Year marking the first day of the Bengali calendar (Poila = first, Boishakh = first month). Celebrated across West Bengal with processions, fairs, traditional attire (women in saris, men in kurtas), family gatherings, and cultural performances. UNESCO recognised this festival as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (2016).
significance: Poila Boishakh represents Bengali cultural and seasonal renewal, rooted in Mughal-era tax collection traditions and evolved into a secular, multi-faith celebration. It is the cornerstone of Bengali cultural identity.

name: Poush Mela
approximate_date: December (7th day of Poush month; typically Dec 21-24)
description: Three-day fair (extended to six days from 2017 onwards) at Tagore's Visva-Bharati University, founded in 1894 to celebrate the establishment anniversary of Brahma Mandir temple. Features approximately 1,500 vendor stalls, live Bengali folk music (baul, kirtan, kobigan), local handicrafts, printed fabrics, and performances. Attracts ~10,000 tourists annually.
significance: Poush Mela is integral to Rabindranath Tagore's vision for Shantiniketan as a centre of cultural expression. The fair celebrates Bengali folk traditions and has been held continuously since 1894 (except during 1943 Bengal Famine, 1946 Direct Action Day, and COVID-19).

name: Basanta Utsav (Spring Festival)
approximate_date: March (first day of Bengali month Falgun; typically mid-March)
description: Spring festival celebrating the arrival of spring (Basanta = spring, Utsav = festival), established in 1923 at Visva-Bharati. Shantiniketan hosts the largest celebration, featuring Rabindra Sangeet (Tagore's compositions), group singing and dancing, coloured powder play (abir), traditional attire, and community processions. The festival blends Holi traditions with Bengali cultural elements.
significance: Basanta Utsav was initiated by Shamindranath Tagore (son of Rabindranath) and elevated to a major Bengali cultural event by the poet himself. It is intrinsic to Tagore's vision of cultural renaissance at Shantiniketan.

name: Adi Kailash Yatra (Pilgrimage Season)
description: Sacred pilgrimage to Adi Kailash (5,945m), known as Chhota (small) Kailash, located in Pithoragarh district near the Indo-Tibetan border. The yatra involves rituals and prayers at Parvati Tal (glacial lake) and Om Parvat, accessible to pilgrims aged 5-80 via BRO motorable roads. Pilgrims seek blessings for marital bliss, harmony, and spiritual growth. Inner Line Permit (ILP) required for Indian citizens.
significance: Adi Kailash is the second most sacred peak among Panch Kailash (five sacred peaks), revered as the secondary home of Lord Shiva and a replica of Mount Kailash in Tibet. 2026 is the Tibetan Year of the Horse, considered extraordinarily auspicious for the kora (pilgrimage).

name: Saga Dawa Festival & Kailash-Mansarovar Yatra
approximate_date: May-June (lunar calendar; Saga Dawa typically May-June)
description: Sacred pilgrimage season to Mount Kailash (6,638m) and Lake Mansarovar (highest freshwater lake globally, 4,590m) in Tibet. The Saga Dawa Festival (May-June), coinciding with Buddha Purnima, honours Sakyamuni Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and nirvana. Thousands of Tibetan pilgrims perform the Kora (circumambulation; 52 km around the mountain), witnessed by the Tarboche prayer pole raising ceremony. 2026 (Tibetan Year of the Horse) carries the spiritual merit of thirteen Koras at any other time.
significance: Kailash-Mansarovar is one of the holiest pilgrimage sites in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions. The best season (May-Oct) offers mild weather and open trekking passes. Saga Dawa is the most auspicious time, drawing pilgrims worldwide.

name: Baisakhi and Janmashtami Fair
description: Nandaprayag, the confluence of Alaknanda and Nandakini rivers, hosts fairs during Baisakhi (spring harvest) and Janmashtami (Krishna's birth). The Gopalji temple, dedicated to Lord Krishna in his child form, is the central place of worship. Pilgrims gather for ritual ablutions (snan), temple ceremonies, and offerings.
significance: Nandaprayag is the second highest among the five sacred river confluences (Panch Prayag) in Garhwal Himalayas. The destination is a pilgrimage stop on the route to Badrinath.

name: Osla Mela & Someshwara Festival
description: Annual festival welcoming Lord Someshwara (a form of Shiva) during the monsoon season in the Har Ki Doon valley. Local drummers (Dhaki) play traditional drums, believed to echo through the valley during festival months. The Osla Mela celebrates local customs, rituals, and traditional cuisine. The ancient Someshwar Devta Temple in the village of Osla is the spiritual centre.
significance: The valley (meaning 'Valley of Gods') holds deep spiritual significance for Shiva worship. The festival connects the local community to their deity and agricultural cycles.

name: Harela Mela (Monsoon Festival)
description: Traditional Kumaoni harvest festival marking the onset of monsoon and the sowing season. Held at Ramleela Ground in Bhimtal, participants plant barley seeds in small pots (symbolising prosperity and good harvest). The festival celebrates agricultural cycles and spiritual renewal rooted in Himalayan traditions.
significance: Harela Mela is deeply embedded in Kumaoni culture and agrarian heritage, representing the community's connection to seasonal cycles and land stewardship.

name: Losar (Tibetan New Year)
description: Tibetan New Year celebration marked by vibrant processions, masked dances, and cultural performances. Celebrated by the significant Tibetan Buddhist community in Kalimpong, featuring monastery prayers, traditional dress, and community gatherings.
significance: Losar is the major festival for Kalimpong's Tibetan Buddhist population, reflecting the town's religious diversity and cultural heritage.

name: Bonbibi Mela (Forest Goddess Festival)
description: Annual festival honouring Bonbibi, the divine protector goddess of the Sundarbans mangrove forest. Celebrated with folk theatre, music, and dance performances narrating the legends of Bonbibi's protection of humans from tigers and forest dangers. Arranged with theatrics, music, and cultural programs.
significance: Bonbibi Mela celebrates the unique syncretism of Hindu and Islamic traditions in Sundarbans culture, representing human-wildlife harmony and the goddess's symbolic role as protector of the forest community.

name: Ilish Utsav (Hilsa Festival)
description: Food festival celebrating the Hilsa (Ilish) fish, abundant in Sundarbans waters during August-September monsoon season. Features traditional recipes, cooking competitions, and cultural performances. Hilsa is a culturally significant fish in Bengali cuisine and Sundarbans identity.
significance: Ilish Utsav celebrates Sundarbans' unique aquatic ecosystem and Bengali fishing heritage, representing the economic and cultural importance of the Hilsa fish to the region.
